source_text: Λέγω τοίνυν αὖθις ἃ καὶ πρότερον εἴρηκα, πάνυ ματαίως ἀνθρώπους διακεῖσθαι, καὶ μήτε ὑπερβολὴν ὅλως ἐνδέχεσθαι τῶν ἐπινοουμένων πραγμάτων τὴν ματαιότητα. Περιττὸς δέ μοι ὁ κάματος ἐκκλησιάζοντι σοφῶς, ὅτι διδάσκειν ἐπιχειρῶν τὸν λαὸν τοῦτον ἀδιδάκτως καὶ ἀνιάτως ἔχοντα. Δεῖ δὲ ἀνδρὸς γενναίου, πρὸς τὸ συνιέναι λόγους σοφίας δυνηθῆναι. Ἐγὼ δὲ ἤδη πρεσβύτης ὢν, καὶ μακρὸν βίου διελθὼν χρόνον, ἔκαμον εἰς τὸ ἀνευρεῖν τὰ τῷ Θεῷ ἀρεστὰ διὰ τῶν τῆς ἀληθείας μυστηρίων. Ἐπίσταμαί τε ὡς ἐπεγείρει ψυχὰς, καὶ νύττει οὐχ ἧττον τὰ τῶν σοφῶν παραγγέλματα, ἢ διατίθεται σώματα βουκέντρῳ, ἢ ἥλῳ ἐμπερονηθέντα. Δώσουσι δέ τινες τὰ σοφὰ ἐκεῖνα διδάγματα, παρ᾽ ἑνὸς ἀγαθοῦ λαβόντες ποιμένος καὶ διδασκάλου, ὥσπερ ἐξ ἑνὸς στόματος ἅπαντες αὑτοῖς συμφώνως δαψιλέστερον τὰ πιστευθέντα διηγούμενοι. Λόγων δὲ πολλῶν οὐδὲν ὄφελος· οὐδέ σοι συμβουλεύω, ὦ φίλος, ἀνόνητα καταγράφειν τὰ περὶ τὸ προσῆκον, ἐν οἷς τοῦ κάμνειν εἰκῆ ἐστὶν οὐδὲν πλέον. Ἀλλά μοι λοιπὸν ἐπιλόγου δεήσει τοιοῦδέ τινος, ὅτι· Ὦ ἄνθρωποι, ἰδοὺ διαῤῥήδην ὑμῖν καὶ συντόμως προαγορεύω, φοβεῖσθαι μὲν Θεὸν τὸν πάντων δεσπότην τε ὁμοῦ καὶ ἐπόπτην, τηρεῖν δὲ αὐτοῦ καὶ τὰ παραγγέλματα· πείθεσθαι δὲ, πάντα τινὰ μετέπειτα καὶ κριθήσεσθαι, καὶ κατ᾽ ἀξίαν ἀπολήψεσθαι ἔκαστον τῶν αὑτοῦ ἔργων τὴν ἀμοιβὴν ἀγαθῶν τε ὁμοῦ καὶ φαύλων.
thought_title: Closing words: fear God and keep His commandments
orientation: Solomon closes the book: fear God and keep His commandments, for every person will be judged.
pass_a_gloss: I say therefore again what I have said also before: that humans are disposed altogether vainly, and that the vanity of the things devised admits no excess at all. Superfluous to me is the toil as I preach in assembly wisely, because (I am) attempting to teach this people, being untaught and incurable. There is need of a noble man to be able to understand words of wisdom. I being already an old man, and having gone through a long time of life, toiled to find out the things pleasing to God through the mysteries of the truth. And I know that the precepts of the wise rouse souls and prick no less than bodies pierced through by an ox goad or a nail are affected. Some will give those wise teachings, having received from one good shepherd and teacher, as from one mouth all in harmony with themselves more abundantly recounting the things entrusted. Of many words there is no profit; nor do I advise you, O friend, to write down profitless things concerning the fitting, in which there is nothing more than toiling in vain. But for me further there will be need of some such epilogue: O humans, behold, expressly and concisely I proclaim to you, to fear God, the Master and at once Overseer of all, and to keep His commandments; and to be persuaded that everyone will afterward also be judged, and each will receive back according to worth the recompense of his own works, good and base alike.

pass_b_english: So I say again what I have said before: human beings are in a state of utter emptiness, and the emptiness of the things they devise could not be greater (Ecclesiastes 12:8). My labor is wasted as I preach wisely to the assembly, since I am trying to teach this people, who are unteachable and past cure (Ecclesiastes 12:9). It takes a man of noble spirit to be able to understand words of wisdom. Now that I am old and have passed through a long span of life, I have labored to find out what is pleasing to God through the mysteries of the truth (Ecclesiastes 12:10). I know that the precepts of the wise rouse souls and prick them no less than bodies are stirred when pierced by an ox goad or a nail (Ecclesiastes 12:11). Some will hand on those wise teachings, having received them from one good Shepherd and Teacher (Ecclesiastes 12:11); all of them, as if from one mouth, will set out more fully, in agreement with one another, what has been entrusted to them.

There is no profit in many words (Ecclesiastes 12:12). Nor do I advise you, my friend, to write down useless things about what is fitting, in which there is nothing more than labor spent in vain (Ecclesiastes 12:12). It remains for me to add a conclusion such as this: O people, here I declare to you plainly and briefly: fear God, the Master and Overseer of all things, and keep His commandments (Ecclesiastes 12:13). And be persuaded that every person will afterward be judged, and that each will receive, as he deserves, the recompense of his own works, good and bad alike (Ecclesiastes 12:14).
notes: Metaphrase of Ecclesiastes 12:8-14, the end of the work. Reads ἃ (relative) as corrected in the source row. 'I am trying' supplies the finite verb missing in both prints after ὅτι διδάσκειν ἐπιχειρῶν. 'Preach wisely to the assembly' renders ἐκκλησιάζοντι, the verb behind the book's title (the Preacher). 'Could not be greater' renders 'admits no excess at all'. 'One good Shepherd and Teacher' is capitalized because, as in Ecclesiastes 12:11 ('one shepherd'), it names the divine source of the teaching; a possible echo of John 10:11 is left uncited. Doubtful: τὰ περὶ τὸ προσῆκον is unclear; it is rendered literally, 'about what is fitting'. Checked against the 1622 Latin (p. 96 A): it has 'ea, quae minus conueniunt' ('things that are less fitting'), as if reading παρά for περί; the English keeps the printed περί, and the doubt stays noted here. 'Good and bad alike' renders ἀγαθῶν τε ὁμοῦ καὶ φαύλων; the wording φαῦλος is close to 2 Corinthians 5:10, but that echo is left uncited as uncertain. No Psalm citations. 'Unteachable and past cure' renders ἀδιδάκτως καὶ ἀνιάτως ἔχοντα (Latin 'ut nec doctrinam nec curationem admittat'). 'Here I declare to you' renders ἰδοὺ ... προαγορεύω (Latin 'en vobis ... denuncio').
